{{short description|Scientific theory}}
In [[physics]], '''Langevin dynamics''' is an approach to the mathematical modeling of the [[dynamics (physics)|dynamics]] of molecular systems using the [[Langevin equation]]. It was originally developed by French physicist [[Paul Langevin]]. The approach is characterized by the use of simplified models while accounting for omitted [[Degrees of freedom (physics and chemistry)|degrees of freedom]] by the use of [[stochastic differential equation]]s. Langevin dynamics simulations are a kind of [[Monte Carlo simulation]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Namiki|first=Mikio|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MVryCAAAQBAJ&q=langevin+simulations+a+kind+of+monte+carlo&pg=PA176|title=Stochastic Quantization|date=2008-10-04|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-3-540-47217-9|language=en|pages=176}}</ref>

== Overview ==
Real world molecular systems occur in air or solvents, rather than in isolation, in a vacuum. Jostling of solvent or air molecules causes friction, and the occasional high velocity collision will perturb the system. Langevin dynamics attempts to extend [[molecular dynamics]] to allow for these effects. Also, Langevin dynamics allows temperature to be controlled as with a thermostat, thus approximating the [[canonical ensemble]].

Langevin dynamics mimics the viscous aspect of a solvent. It does not fully model an [[implicit solvent]]; specifically, the model does not account for the [[Poisson-Boltzmann equation|electrostatic screening]] and also not for the [[hydrophobic effect]]. For denser solvents, hydrodynamic interactions are not captured via Langevin dynamics.

For a system of <math>N</math> particles with masses <math>M</math>, with coordinates <math>X=X(t)</math> that constitute a time-dependent [[random variable]], the resulting [[Langevin equation]] is<ref>{{cite book | first=Tamar | last=Schlick | authorlink= Tamar Schlick | year=2002 | title=Molecular Modeling and Simulation | publisher=Springer | isbn=0-387-95404-X |  page = 480 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last1=Pastor | first1=R.W. | year = 1994 | chapter = Techniques and Applications of Langevin Dynamics Simulations | editor1-last = Luckhurst | editor1-first = G.R. | editor2-last = Veracini | editor2-first = C.A. | title = The Molecular Dynamics of Liquid Crystals |series=NATO ASI Series|volume=431|pages=85–138 |publisher= Springer |location=Dordrecht|doi=10.1007/978-94-011-1168-3_5 |isbn=978-94-010-4509-4 }}</ref>
<math display="block">M\,\ddot{\mathbf{X}} = - \mathbf{\nabla} U(\mathbf{X}) - \gamma\,M\,\dot{\mathbf{X}} + \sqrt{2\,M\,\gamma\,k_{\rm B} T}\,\mathbf{R}(t)\,,</math>
where <math>U(\mathbf{X})</math> is the particle interaction potential; <math>\nabla</math> is the gradient operator such that <math>-\mathbf{\nabla} U(\mathbf{X})</math> is the force calculated from the particle interaction potentials; the dot is a [[time derivative]] such that <math>\dot{\mathbf{X}}</math> is the velocity and <math>\ddot{\mathbf{X}}</math> is the acceleration; <math>\gamma</math> is the damping constant (units of reciprocal time), also known as the [[collision frequency]]; <math>T</math> is the temperature, <math>k_{\rm B}</math> is the [[Boltzmann constant]]; and <math>\mathbf{R}(t)</math> is a delta-correlated [[Stationary process|stationary]] [[Gaussian Process|Gaussian process]] with zero-mean, called Gaussian [[white noise]], satisfying
<math display="block">\left\langle \mathbf{R}(t) \right\rangle = 0</math>
<math display="block">\left\langle \mathbf{R}(t)\cdot\mathbf{R}(t') \right\rangle = \delta(t - t')</math>

Here, <math>\delta</math> is the [[Dirac delta]].
=== Stochastic Differential Formulation ===

Considering the [[covariance]] of [[standard Brownian motion]] or [[Wiener process]] <math>W_t</math>, we can find that 

<math display="block"> \mathbb{E}(W_tW_\tau) = \min(t,\tau) </math>

Define the covariance matrix of the derivative as
<math display="block">\mathbb{E}(\dot{W_t}\dot{W_\tau}) =  \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\frac{\partial}{\partial \tau}\mathbb{E}(W_tW_\tau) = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\frac{\partial}{\partial \tau}\min(t,\tau) =\delta(t-\tau) </math>
So under the sense of [[covariance]] we can say that

<math display="block">{\rm d}W_t = \mathbf{R}(t){\rm d}t</math>
[[Without loss of generality]], let the mass <math>M = 1</math>, <math>\sigma = \sqrt{M\gamma k_{\rm B}T}</math>, then the original SDE will become
<math display="block">  {\rm d}\dot{\mathbf{X}} = -\nabla U(\mathbf{X}){\rm d}t-\gamma {\rm d}{\mathbf{X}} +\sqrt{2}\sigma{\rm d} \mathbf{W}(t) </math>

=== Overdamped Langevin dynamics === 
If the main objective is to control temperature, care should be exercised to use a small damping constant <math>\gamma</math>. As <math>\gamma</math> grows, it spans from the inertial all the way to the diffusive ([[Brownian motion|Brownian]]) regime. The Langevin dynamics limit of non-inertia is commonly described as [[Brownian dynamics]]. Brownian dynamics can be considered as overdamped Langevin dynamics, i.e. Langevin dynamics where no average acceleration takes place. Under this limit we have <math>{\rm d}\dot{X}=0</math>, the original SDE then will becomes

<math display="block">  {\rm d}{\mathbf{X}} =-\frac{1}{\gamma}\nabla U(\mathbf{X}){\rm d}t+\frac{\sqrt{2}\sigma}{\gamma}{\rm d} \mathbf{W}(t) </math> 

The translational Langevin equation can be solved using various numerical methods <ref>{{Cite journal
 |last1=Tanygin

 |language=en

 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal

The Langevin equation can be generalized to [[Rotation|rotational]] dynamics of [[molecule]]s, [[Brownian motion|Brownian]] particles, ''etc.'' A standard (according to [[National Institute of Standards and Technology|NIST]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Martys |first1=Nicos S. |last2=Mountain |first2=Raymond D. |date=1999-03-01 |title=Velocity Verlet algorithm for dissipative-particle-dynamics-based models of suspensions |url=https://journals.aps.org/pre/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevE.59.3733 |journal=Physical Review E |language=en |volume=59 |issue=3 |pages=3733 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.59.3733 |issn=1063-651X }}</ref>) way to do it is to leverage a [[quaternion]]-based description of the stochastic rotational motion.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Omelyan |first=Igor P. |date=1998-01-01 |title=On the numerical integration of motion for rigid polyatomics: The modified quaternion approach |url=https://pubs.aip.org/cip/article/12/1/97/136748/On-the-numerical-integration-of-motion-for-rigid |journal=Computers in Physics |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=97–103 |doi=10.1063/1.168642 |issn=0894-1866|arxiv=physics/9901028 |bibcode=1998ComPh..12...97O }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Groot |first1=Robert D. |last2=Warren |first2=Patrick B. |date=1997-09-15 |title=Dissipative particle dynamics: Bridging the gap between atomistic and mesoscopic simulation |url=https://pubs.aip.org/jcp/article/107/11/4423/478600/Dissipative-particle-dynamics-Bridging-the-gap |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=107 |issue=11 |pages=4423–4435 |doi=10.1063/1.474784 |bibcode=1997JChPh.107.4423G |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Applications ==

=== Langevin thermostat ===
Langevin thermostat<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Allen |first1=Michael P. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WFExDwAAQBAJ&pg=PP1 |title=Computer Simulation of Liquids |last2=Tildesley |first2=Dominic J. |date=2017-08-15 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-252470-6 |language=en}}</ref> is a type of [[Thermostat]] algorithm in [[molecular dynamics]], which is used to simulate a [[canonical ensemble]] (NVT) under a desired temperature. It integrates the following Langevin equation of motion:

<math>M \ddot{\mathbf{X}} = -\nabla U(\mathbf{X}) - \gamma \dot{\mathbf{X}} + \sqrt{2\gamma k_BT} \textbf{R}(t)</math>

<math>-\nabla U(\mathbf{X})</math> is the deterministic force term; <math>\gamma</math> is the friction coefficient and <math>\gamma \dot{X}</math> is the friction or damping term; the last term is the random force term (<math>k_B</math>: [[Boltzmann constant]], <math>T</math>: temperature). This equation allows the system to couple with an imaginary "heat bath": the kinetic energy of the system dissipates from the friction/damping term, and gain from random force/fluctuation; the strength of coupling is controlled by <math>\gamma</math>. This equation can be simulated with [[Stochastic differential equation|SDE]] solvers such as [[Euler–Maruyama method]], where the random force term is replaced by a [[Gaussian random variable|Gaussian random number]] in every integration step (variance <math>\sigma^2 = 2\gamma k_BT/ \Delta t</math>, <math>\Delta t</math>: time step), or Langevin [[Leapfrog integration]], etc. This method is also known as Langevin Integrator.<ref>{{Cite web |title=21. Integrators — OpenMM User Guide 8.2 documentation |url=http://docs.openmm.org/latest/userguide/theory/04_integrators.html#integrators-theory |access-date=2025-05-12 |website=docs.openmm.org}}</ref>

=== Langevin Monte Carlo ===
The [[Brownian dynamics|overdamped Langevin equation]] gives

<math>{\rm d} \mathbf{x}_t = - \frac{D}{k_BT} \nabla_\mathbf{x} U(\mathbf{x}_t) {\rm d}t + \sqrt{2D}  {\rm d} W_t</math>

Here, <math>D = k_B T / \gamma</math> is the [[diffusion coefficient]] from [[Einstein relation (kinetic theory)|Einstein relation]]'''.''' As proven with [[Fokker–Planck equation|Fokker-Planck equation]], under appropriate conditions, the [[stationary distribution]] of <math>\mathbf x_t</math> is [[Boltzmann distribution]] <math>p(\mathbf{x}) \propto e^{-U(\mathbf{x})/k_BT}</math>.

Since that <math>\nabla \log p(\mathbf{x})=-\nabla U(\mathbf{x})/k_BT</math>, this equation is equivalent to the following form:

<math>{\rm d} \mathbf{x}_t = \epsilon \nabla_\mathbf{x}\log p(\mathbf x_t) {\rm d}t + \sqrt{2\epsilon} {\rm d} W_t</math>

And the distribution of <math>\mathbf x_t (t\to \infty)</math> follows <math>p(\mathbf{x})</math>. In other words, Langevin dynamics drives particles towards a stationary distribution <math>p(\mathbf{x})</math> along a gradient flow, due to the <math>\nabla \log p(\mathbf{x})</math> term, while still allowing for some random fluctuations. This provides a [[Markov chain Monte Carlo|Markov Chain Monte Carlo]] method that can be used to sample data <math>\mathbf x</math> from a target distribution <math>p(\mathbf{x})</math>, known as [[Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm|Langevin Monte Carlo]].

In many applications, we have a desired distribution <math>p(\mathbf{x})</math> from which we would like to sample <math>\mathbf x</math>, but direct sampling might be challenging or inefficient. Langevin Monte Carlo offers another way to sample <math>\mathbf x \sim p(\mathbf x)</math> by sampling a [[Markov chain]] in accordance with the Langevin dynamics whose [[stationary state]] is <math>p(\mathbf{x})</math>. The [[Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm]] (MALA) is an example : Given a current state <math>\mathbf x_t</math>, the MALA method proposes a new state <math>\tilde{x}_{t+1}</math> using the Langevin dynamics above. The proposal is then accepted or rejected based on the [[Metropolis–Hastings algorithm|Metropolis-Hastings algorithm]]. The incorporation of the Langevin dynamics in the choice of <math>\tilde{x}_{t+1}</math> provides greater computational efficiency, since the dynamics drive the particles into regions of higher <math>p(\mathbf{x})</math> probability and are thus more likely to be accepted. Read more in [[Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm]].

=== Score-based generative model ===
Langevin dynamics is one of the bases of [[Diffusion model#Score-based generative model|score-based generative models]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> From (overdamped) Langevin dynamics,

<math>{\rm d} \mathbf{x}_t = \epsilon \nabla_\mathbf{x}
\log p(\mathbf x_t) {\rm d}t + \sqrt{2\epsilon} {\rm d} W_t</math>

A [[generative model]] aims to generate samples that follow (unknown data distribution) <math>p(\mathbf{x})</math>. To achieve that, a score-based model learns an approximate [[Score (statistics)|score function]] <math>\mathbf{s}_\theta(\mathbf{x}) \approx \nabla_\mathbf{x} \log p(\mathbf{x})</math> (a process called [[Diffusion model#Score matching|score matching]]). With access to a score function, samples are generated by the following iteration,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution {{!}} Yang Song |url=https://yang-song.net/blog/2021/score/ |access-date=2025-05-12 |website=yang-song.net}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite arXiv | eprint=2011.13456 | last1=Song | first1=Yang | last2=Sohl-Dickstein | first2=Jascha | last3=Kingma | first3=Diederik P. | last4=Kumar | first4=Abhishek | last5=Ermon | first5=Stefano | last6=Poole | first6=Ben | title=Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations | date=2020 | class=cs.LG }}</ref>

<math>\mathbf{x}_{i+1} \gets \mathbf{x}_i + \epsilon \nabla_\mathbf{x} \log p(\mathbf{x}_i) + \sqrt{2\epsilon} \mathbf{z}_i,
\quad i=0,1,\cdots, K</math>

with <math>\mathbf{z}_i \sim N(0,1)</math>. As <math>\epsilon \to 0</math> and <math>K \to \infty</math>, the generated <math>\mathbf{x}_K</math> converge to the target distribution <math>p(\mathbf x)</math>. Score-based models use <math>\mathbf{s}_\theta(\mathbf{x}) \approx \nabla_\mathbf{x} \log p(\mathbf{x})</math> as an approximation.<ref name=":0" />

== Relation to Other Theories ==
=== Klein-Kramers equation ===
As a [[stochastic differential equation]](SDE), '''Langevin dynamics''' equation, has its corresponding [[partial differential equation]](PDE), [[ Klein-Kramers equation]], a special [[Fokker–Planck equation]] that governs the [[probability distribution]] of the particles in the [[phase space]]. The original '''Langevin dynamics''' equation can be reformulated as the following first order SDEs:
<math display="block">  {\rm d}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{P}{\rm d} t </math>
<math display="block"> {\rm d} \mathbf{P} = -\gamma\mathbf{P}{\rm d}t-\nabla U(\mathbf{X}){\rm d} t+\sqrt{2}\sigma {\rm d}\mathbf{W}(t) </math>
Now consider the following cases and their law of <math>(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{P})</math>:

1.<math>\mathbf{{\rm d}{X}} = \mathbf{P}{\rm d} t
            , \mathbf{{\rm d}{P}} = -\gamma\mathbf{P}{\rm d} t-\nabla U(\mathbf{X}){\rm d} t+\sqrt{2}\sigma {\rm d}\mathbf{W}(t) </math> with <math> (\mathbf{X}_0,\mathbf{P}_0)\sim\rho_0 </math>

2. <math> \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} = -\mathbf{P}\nabla_{\mathbf{X}}\rho+\nabla_{\mathbf{P}}(\gamma\mathbf{P}\rho+\nabla_{\mathbf{X}}U(\mathbf{X})\rho)+\nabla_{\mathbf{P}}^2(\sigma_{T}^2\rho) </math> with <math> \rho(t=0,\mathbf{X},\mathbf{P})=\rho_0 </math>

Consider a general function of momentum and position

<math display="block">  \Psi_t = \Psi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{P})  </math>

The expectation value of the function will be

<math display="block">  \mathbb{E}[\Psi_t] = \int \rho(t,\mathbf{X},\mathbf{P})\Psi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{P}){\rm d} \mathbf{P}{\rm d} \mathbf{X} </math>

Taking derivative with respect to time <math>t</math>, and applying [[Itô's formula]], we have
<math display="block">   \mathbb{E}[\frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t}\Psi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{P})] 
            =\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{\mathbf{X}} \Psi\frac{{\rm d}\mathbf{X}}{{\rm d}t} + \nabla_{\mathbf{P}}\Psi\frac{{\rm d}\mathbf{P}}{{\rm d}t} + \sigma_T^2\nabla_{\mathbf{P}}^2\Psi\frac{1}{{\rm d} t}({\rm d} \mathbf{W}(t))^2]</math>
which can be simplified to 
<math display="block"> \int (\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\rho)\Psi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{P}){\rm d} \mathbf{X}{\rm d}\mathbf{P} =\mathbb{E}[(\nabla_{\mathbf{X}} \Psi)\mathbf{P} + \nabla_{\mathbf{P}}\Psi(-\gamma\mathbf{P}-\nabla_{\mathbf{X}}U(\mathbf{X})) + \sigma_T^2\nabla_{\mathbf{P}}^2\Psi]</math>
[[Integration by parts]] on right hand side, due to vanishing density for infinite momentum or velocity we have
<math display="block"> (\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\rho)\Psi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{P}){\rm d} \mathbf{X}{\rm d}\mathbf{P} = \int(-\mathbf{P}\nabla_{\mathbf{X}}\rho+\nabla_{\mathbf{P}}(\gamma\mathbf{P}\rho+\nabla_{\mathbf{X}}U(\mathbf{X})\rho)+\nabla_{\mathbf{P}}^2(\sigma_{T}^2\rho) )\Psi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{P}){\rm d}\mathbf{X}{\rm d}\mathbf{P} </math>
This equation holds for arbitrary <math>\Psi</math>, so we require the density to satisfy
<math display="block"> \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} = -\mathbf{P}\nabla_{\mathbf{X}}\rho+\nabla_{\mathbf{P}}(\gamma\mathbf{P}\rho+\nabla_{\mathbf{X}}U(\mathbf{X})\rho)+\nabla_{\mathbf{P}}^2(\sigma_{T}^2\rho)</math>
This equation is called the [[Klein-Kramers equation]], a special version of [[Fokker Planck equation]]. It's a partial differential equation that describes the evolution of probability density of the system in the phase space.
=== Fokker Planck equation ===
For the overdamped limit,  we have <math>{\rm d}\mathbf{P} = 0</math>, so the evolution of system can be reduced to the position subspace. Following similar logic we can prove that the SDE for position, 
<math display="block">{\rm d} \mathbf{X} = -\frac{1}{\gamma}\nabla U(\mathbf{X}){\rm d} t +\sqrt{2}\frac{\sigma}{\gamma}\mathbf{R}(t){\rm d} t</math> 
corresponds to the [[Fokker Planck equation]] for probability density 
<math display="block"> \frac{\partial \rho(t,\mathbf{X})}{\partial t} = \nabla_{\mathbf{X}}(\frac{1}{\gamma}\nabla_{\mathbf{X}}U(\mathbf{X})\rho(t,\mathbf{X}))+\Delta_\mathbf{X}(\frac{\sigma^2}{\gamma^2}\rho(t,\mathbf{X}))</math>
=== Fluctuation-dissipation theorem  ===
Consider Langevin dynamics of a [[free particle]] (i.e. <math> U(\mathbf{X})=0 </math>), then the equation for momentum will become

<math display="block"> {\rm d}\mathbf{P} = -\frac{1}{\gamma} \mathbf{P}{\rm d}t +\frac{\sqrt{2}\sigma}{\gamma} {\rm d}\mathbf{W}_t </math>

the analytical solution to this [[stochastic differential equation|SDE]] is 

<math display="block">\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{P}_0e^{- t/\gamma}+\frac{\sqrt{2}\sigma}{\gamma}\int_0^t {\rm e}^{-(t-t')/\gamma}{\rm d}\mathbf{W}_t'</math> 
thus the average value of [[second moment]] of momentum will becomes (here we apply the [[Itô isometry]])
<math display="block">\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{P}^2) = \mathbf{P}^2_0{\rm e}^{-2 t/\gamma}+ \frac{\sigma^2}{\gamma}(1-{\rm e}^{-2t/\gamma})\overset{t\to\infty}{\to}\frac{\sigma^2}{\gamma}  </math>
That is, the limiting behavior when time approaches positive infinity, the momentum fluctuation of this system is related to the energy dissipation ([[friction]] term parameter <math> \gamma </math>) of this system. Combining this result with [[Equipartition theorem]], which relates the average value of [[kinetic energy]] of particles with [[temperature]]

<math display="block"> \langle v^2\rangle = k_{\rm B}T </math>

we can determines the value of the variance <math> \sigma </math> in applications like Langevin thermostat.

<math display="block">\sigma^2/\gamma = k_B T \to \sigma = \sqrt{k_{\rm B} T\gamma}</math>
This is consistent with the original definition assuming <math>M=1</math>.

=== Path integral ===
[[Path integral formulation]] comes from [[quantum mechanics]]. But for a Langevin SDE we can also induce a corresponding path integral. Considering the following overdamped Langevin equation under, where without loss of generality we take <math>\gamma = \sigma = 1  </math>,

<math display="block"> {\rm d}{X} = -\nabla U({X}){\rm d}t +\sqrt{2}{\rm d}W_t </math>

Discretize and define <math> t_n = n\Delta t </math>, we get

<math display="block"> {X}_{n+1} -{X}_{n} + \nabla U({X})\Delta t=   \sqrt{2}(W_{t_n}-W_{t_{n-1}})\sim \mathcal{N}(0,2\sqrt{\Delta t}) </math>
Therefore the propagation probability will be
<math display="block"> P({X}_{n+1}|{X}_{n}) = \int {\rm d}\xi \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi\Delta t}}{\rm e}^{-\frac{\xi^2}{4\Delta t}} \delta({X}_{n+1} -{X}_{n} + \nabla U({X})\Delta t-\xi)</math>
Applying [[Fourier Transform]] of [[delta function]], and we will get
<math display="block"> P = \int \frac{{\rm d}k}{2\pi}{\rm e}^{{\rm i}k({X}_{n+1}-{X}_n + \nabla U({X})\Delta t)}\int {\rm d}\xi \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi\Delta t}}{\rm e}^{-\frac{\xi^2}{4\Delta t}}{\rm e}^{-{\rm i}k\xi}  </math>
The second part is a [[Gaussian Integral]], which yields 
<math display="block"> P = \int \frac{{\rm d}k}{2\pi}{\rm e}^{{\rm i}k({X}_{n+1}-{X}_n + \nabla U({X})\Delta t)}{\rm e}^{-k^2\Delta t} </math>
Now consider the probability from initial <math>X_0</math>
to final <math>X_n</math>. 
<math display="block"> P(\mathbf{X}_n|\mathbf{X}_0) = \int \frac{1}{2\pi}\prod_i^{N-1} {\rm d}k_i {\rm e}^{({\rm i}k_i(\dot{X} + \nabla U(X))-k_i^2)\Delta t} </math>
take the limit of <math>\Delta t\to 0</math>,we will get
<math display="block"> P(\mathbf{X}_n|\mathbf{X}_0) = \int \mathcal{D}[k] {\rm e}^{\int_0^{t_n}({\rm i}k(\dot{X} + \nabla U(X))-k^2){\rm d} t} </math>
